explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The psalm says, "Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) Picture shoving a mountain. You'd pull something before it budged an inch, and I'd be the guy cheering from the sidelines with a sore mustache.

I get why a mountain makes you think "biggest," friend. But the psalm never mentions height. It says Mount Zion "…cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) The picture is about staying put, not winning a tallest-peak contest. That's the quality the psalm says belongs to people who trust the LORD.

Green is a nice guess, friend, but the psalm doesn't mention it. What it says about Mount Zion is, "It cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) That's the quality the picture is built on. Steady, no matter what comes at it. Colors never come up.

Careful, friend, this one's flipped. The psalm says the opposite: Mount Zion "…cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) A season is about how long a fresh tray of my cookies lasts once somebody walks past the counter. Forever is a whole other category. The psalm says the people who trust the LORD are like that mountain.

Right, baker. The psalm says Mount Zion "…cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) So a season is far too short for what the verse describes. Nobody ever called a mountain a limited-time offer. And the psalm says those who trust in the LORD are like it.

Yes! "As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people…" (Psalm 125:2) Think of the mountains standing all the way around the city. That's the picture of how the LORD surrounds them. I'd say that's a pretty great place to be standing.

Priests are a fair guess, baker, but they aren't in this verse. It says, "As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people…" (Psalm 125:2) His people, all of them. Nobody's left out of that circle.

I see why you'd pick king, but the psalm doesn't say that here. The verse reads, "As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people…" (Psalm 125:2) His people is the whole crowd, friend. Nobody is singled out, and nobody is left outside the circle.

That's it, baker. The psalm says the LORD surrounds His people "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 125:2) That covers today and every day after it. I've stamped plenty of cookies that didn't last the afternoon, and this lasts forevermore. It's one promise with no end date.

That sounds sensible, friend, but the psalm doesn't put any condition on it. It says the LORD surrounds His people "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 125:2) Nothing in the verse says it stops when a danger passes. The verse gives now and forevermore, and that's all.

explanations.answer: As long as the city stands
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but the psalm doesn't tie it to the city. It says the LORD surrounds His people "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 125:2) The mountains are the picture. The forevermore is what the verse says.

explanations.answer: So the righteous won't turn to injustice
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says the scepter of the wicked will not rest on the land, "…so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice." (Psalm 125:3) That's the reason the psalm gives. The scepter is the wicked ruler's staff of power. The psalm says it won't settle on the land given to the righteous.

explanations.answer: So the righteous can grow their harvest
explanations.explanation: Harvest is a nice thought, baker, but this verse doesn't mention one. The reason it gives is right there: "…so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice." (Psalm 125:3) That's the "why" the psalm states. It's about what the righteous will not do, not what they will grow.

explanations.answer: So the wicked will turn and repent
explanations.explanation: I like your heart on that one, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. The reason it gives is "…so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice." (Psalm 125:3) The verse says nothing about the wicked turning around. Its reason is about the righteous.

That's right, baker. The psalm prays, "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart." (Psalm 125:4) The psalm is speaking straight to the LORD here. The ask is simply that He do good to them.

Long life sounds lovely, baker, but it's not what the psalm asks here. The prayer is, "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart." (Psalm 125:4) The psalm speaks right to the LORD in this verse. What it asks for is that He do good to them.

Great names, ha! Nice guess, friend, but that's not in this verse. The psalm says, "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart." (Psalm 125:4) The request is for the LORD to do good to them.

Yes, baker. The psalm says, "But those who turn to crooked ways the LORD will banish with the evildoers." (Psalm 125:5) I think this is a heavy line. It comes right after the prayer, "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart." (Psalm 125:4)

Not this time, friend. The psalm does say it: "But those who turn to crooked ways the LORD will banish with the evildoers." (Psalm 125:5) I think it's a heavy line, and the psalm doesn't soften it. It's followed right away by "Peace be upon Israel." (Psalm 125:5)
